meaning: The observed statistic is, for example, the difference in mean score between two models. Under the null hypothesis that the models are interchangeable, each item's pair of outputs can be swapped at random (paired approximate randomization) or group labels shuffled; B random permutations build the null distribution. Makes no normality assumption and works for any metric.
used_for: Significance testing for NLP system comparisons (approximate randomization for BLEU, F1 and accuracy), A/B tests with unusual metrics, neuroscience-style analyses of model activations. Book: only here.

name: Multiple-comparison corrections (Bonferroni, Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg)
formula: Bonferroni: reject if p_i ≤ α ÷ m ; Benjamini-Hochberg: sort p-values p_(1) ≤ ... ≤ p_(m), find the largest k with p_(k) ≤ (k ÷ m) × α, reject hypotheses 1..k
meaning: m is the number of hypotheses tested (model pairs, benchmarks, metrics, A/B variants); α (alpha) is the target error rate; p_i are p-values. Bonferroni controls the chance of any false positive (family-wise error), and Holm is a uniformly more powerful step-down version; Benjamini-Hochberg controls the expected share of false discoveries (false discovery rate) and is less conservative.
used_for: Leaderboards comparing many models at once, A/B platforms testing many metrics, eval suites with dozens of benchmarks, genomics. Book: only here.

name: Rank correlation (Spearman's ρ and Kendall's τ)
formula: Spearman ρ = 1 − 6 × sum over i of d_i^2 ÷ (n × (n^2 − 1)) ; Kendall τ = (C − D) ÷ (n × (n − 1) ÷ 2)
meaning: n is the number of items ranked (for example models); d_i is the difference between item i's two ranks (formula for no ties; otherwise compute Pearson correlation on the ranks); C and D are the numbers of concordant and discordant pairs (pairs ordered the same or opposite way by the two rankings). Both range from −1 to 1.
used_for: Checking whether a cheap benchmark or LLM judge ranks models the same way as human preference (Arena-Hard and MT-Bench validation against Chatbot Arena), agreement between metric and human judgments in MT and summarization, recommender ranking agreement. Book: only here.

name: Item response theory and benchmark-stitching models
formula: P(model i correct on item j) = sigmoid(a_j × (θ_i − b_j)) ; Epoch AI: score(m, b) = sigmoid(α_b × (C_m − D_b))
meaning: θ_i (theta) is model i's ability; b_j is item j's difficulty; a_j its discrimination (slope); sigmoid is the logistic function. The one-parameter (Rasch) model fixes a_j = 1; the three-parameter model adds a guessing floor c_j + (1 − c_j) × sigmoid(...). Epoch AI's aggregate-level version uses each model's capability C_m and each benchmark's difficulty D_b and slope α_b, fit jointly across all models and benchmarks.
used_for: Estimating full-benchmark scores from a small subset of items (tinyBenchmarks, Polo et al., 2024), building aggregate capability indexes: the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) puts models on one scale (rescaled so Claude 3.5 Sonnet = 130 and GPT-5 = 150), from 'A Rosetta Stone for AI Benchmarks' (arXiv 2512.00193). Book: Chapter 24 (Epoch Capabilities Index, aggregate indexes).

name: METR task-completion time horizon
formula: P(agent succeeds on task) = sigmoid(β × (ln(h) − ln(t_task))) ; the 50% time horizon is h
meaning: t_task is how long skilled humans take on the task (geometric mean of human baseline times); h and β (beta) are fitted for each AI agent by logistic regression over many tasks; at t_task = h the success chance is 0.5. The 80% horizon is read off the same curve where it reaches 0.8. Trend: regressing ln(h) on model release date gave a doubling time of about 7 months (207 days, bootstrap 95% interval 166 to 240 days) in METR's March 2025 paper.
used_for: METR's time-horizon measurements of frontier models (Kwa et al., 2025), cited in frontier model and system cards and in forecasts of AI R&D automation. Book: Chapter 24 (METR time horizon), Chapter 21, Chapter 57.

name: N-gram overlap contamination score
formula: contamination(x) = (number of tokens of x that lie inside some n-gram also found in the training corpus) ÷ (number of tokens of x) ; flag x as contaminated if this exceeds a threshold
meaning: x is one benchmark example; an n-gram is a run of n consecutive tokens or words; the training corpus is searched (usually with a suffix array or Bloom filter) for each n-gram of x. Choices of n and threshold vary: GPT-3 used 13-gram overlap; Llama 3 (2024) used 8-gram overlap with a per-benchmark threshold. Scores on clean and contaminated subsets are then compared.
used_for: Decontaminating pretraining data and auditing benchmark results in frontier model reports (GPT-3, Llama 3, and similar analyses in later reports). Book: Chapter 9 (data leakage), Chapter 19 (decontamination), Chapter 24 (benchmark contamination).

name: Neighborhood collaborative filtering (user-based and item-based)
formula: r_hat_ui = mean_u + sum over v in N(u) of sim(u, v) × (r_vi − mean_v) ÷ sum over v in N(u) of |sim(u, v)| ; Pearson sim(u, v) = sum over co-rated items i of (r_ui − mean_u) × (r_vi − mean_v) ÷ sqrt(sum (r_ui − mean_u)^2 × sum (r_vi − mean_v)^2)
meaning: r_ui is user u's rating of item i and r_hat_ui the prediction; mean_u is u's average rating; N(u) are the most similar users who rated i; sim is a similarity (Pearson correlation as shown, or cosine). Item-based collaborative filtering swaps the roles: predict from the user's ratings of items most similar to i, with item-item similarities precomputed.
used_for: Amazon's item-to-item recommendations (Linden et al., 2003), 'people who bought this also bought', baselines in recommender research and small catalogs. Book: Chapter 51 (collaborative filtering: people like you), Chapter 10.

name: Matrix factorization for recommendations (with biases)
formula: r_hat_ui = μ + b_u + b_i + p_u · q_i ; minimize sum over observed (u, i) of (r_ui − r_hat_ui)^2 + λ × (length(p_u)^2 + length(q_i)^2 + b_u^2 + b_i^2) ; SGD step: e = r_ui − r_hat_ui, p_u = p_u + η × (e × q_i − λ × p_u), q_i = q_i + η × (e × p_u − λ × q_i)
meaning: μ (mu) is the global average rating; b_u and b_i are user and item biases (a generous user, a popular item); p_u and q_i are learned k-dimensional factor vectors for user u and item i, whose dot product captures taste match; λ is the L2 penalty; η the learning rate; only observed ratings enter the sum. Truncated SVD of a fully observed matrix (and latent semantic analysis of term-document matrices) is the unregularized relative.
used_for: The Netflix Prize-winning family of models (Koren, Bell and Volinsky, 2009); embedding tables in modern recommenders descend from it. Book: Chapter 51 (matrix factorization: discovering hidden tastes; how the factors are learned), Chapter 10 (recommenders and the Netflix Prize).

name: Alternating least squares (explicit and implicit feedback)
formula: p_u = (Q_u^T × Q_u + λ × I)^(−1) × Q_u^T × r_u ; implicit: minimize sum over all (u, i) of c_ui × (y_ui − p_u · q_i)^2 + λ × (...), with c_ui = 1 + α × r_ui and y_ui = 1 if r_ui > 0 else 0
meaning: Holding item factors fixed, each user's factor vector p_u is a ridge-regression solution: Q_u stacks the factor vectors of items u rated, r_u is u's ratings, λ the penalty, I the identity; then items are solved with users fixed, and the two alternate. For implicit feedback (clicks, plays) r_ui counts interactions, y_ui is the binary preference and c_ui (with scale α) is the confidence; every user-item pair enters the loss, made tractable by an algebraic shortcut.
used_for: Spark MLlib ALS, the implicit library, large-scale industrial recommenders on click and play logs (Hu, Koren and Volinsky, 2008). Book: Chapter 51 (how the factors are learned).

name: Dot-product scoring and the two-tower model
formula: score(u, i) = f(u) · g(i) ; P(i given u) = exp(score(u, i)) ÷ sum over items j of exp(score(u, j))
meaning: f(u) is the user (or query) tower, a network that turns user features and history into a vector; g(i) is the item (or document) tower; the dot product is their match score (cosine if both are normalized). Because item vectors can be computed in advance, the top items for a user are found with maximum-inner-product or nearest-neighbor search. Training typically uses a softmax over items, approximated with in-batch or sampled negatives.
used_for: Candidate generation in YouTube, Google Play, TikTok, Pinterest and other feeds; dense retrieval for search and RAG (bi-encoder embedding models score query · passage); ad retrieval. Book: Chapter 51 (embeddings and the two-tower model; stage 1: candidate generation), Chapter 27.

name: Sampled softmax with logQ correction
formula: s_c(u, i) = s(u, i) − ln(Q(i)) ; loss = −ln(exp(s_c(u, i+)) ÷ sum over j in the batch of exp(s_c(u, j)))
meaning: s(u, i) is the two-tower dot-product score; Q(i) is the probability that item i appears as a sampled negative (with in-batch negatives, roughly its popularity, often estimated by streaming frequency counts); i+ is the item the user actually engaged with; subtracting ln Q(i) removes the bias that popular items are over-sampled as negatives and would otherwise be unfairly penalized.
used_for: Training two-tower retrieval models at YouTube (Yi et al., RecSys 2019) and many industrial recommenders; the same correction appears in sampled-softmax language-model training. Book: only here (Chapter 51 describes two-tower training in words).

name: Factorization machine
formula: y_hat(x) = w_0 + sum over i of w_i × x_i + sum over pairs i < j of (v_i · v_j) × x_i × x_j ; pair term = (1 ÷ 2) × sum over f of [(sum over i of v_(i,f) × x_i)^2 − sum over i of v_(i,f)^2 × x_i^2]
meaning: x is a sparse feature vector (one-hot user, item, context fields); w_0 and w_i are a global bias and per-feature weights; each feature i has a k-dimensional factor vector v_i, and the dot product v_i · v_j models the interaction of features i and j even when that pair was never seen together. The rewritten pair term computes all interactions in time proportional to k × (number of nonzero features).
used_for: Click-through-rate prediction in ads and recommendations (libFM, field-aware FMs in ad competitions), and the FM component of DeepFM-style deep CTR models. Book: only here.

name: Bayesian personalized ranking (BPR) loss
formula: loss = −sum over triples (u, i, j) of ln(sigmoid(x_hat_ui − x_hat_uj)) + λ × length(θ)^2
meaning: Each triple pairs a user u with an item i they interacted with and an item j they did not (sampled); x_hat_ui is the model's score (for example p_u · q_i); θ are all model parameters and λ the L2 penalty. The loss pushes observed items above unobserved ones, optimizing ranking (it is a smooth surrogate for AUC) rather than predicting ratings.
used_for: Implicit-feedback recommenders (Rendle et al., 2009), baselines in recommendation research, pairwise training of retrieval models. Book: only here.

name: Discounted cumulative gain (DCG) and normalized DCG
formula: DCG@k = sum over positions i = 1..k of rel_i ÷ log2(i + 1) (alternative gain: (2^rel_i − 1) ÷ log2(i + 1)) ; NDCG@k = DCG@k ÷ IDCG@k
meaning: rel_i is the graded relevance of the result at position i (for example 0 to 3); log2(i + 1) is the position discount (1 at the top, growing slowly); IDCG@k is the DCG of the ideal ordering (results sorted by relevance), so NDCG runs from 0 to 1. The exponential gain variant emphasizes highly relevant results; libraries and papers differ on which they use.
used_for: Search and recommender evaluation and learning-to-rank objectives; NDCG@10 is the headline retrieval metric of the BEIR and MTEB embedding benchmarks used to compare embedding models for RAG. Book: Chapter 51 (offline metrics; NDCG worked: 3.149 ÷ 4.762 ≈ 0.66).

name: Mean reciprocal rank (MRR)
formula: MRR = (1 ÷ |Q|) × sum over queries q of 1 ÷ rank_q
meaning: Q is the set of queries and |Q| their number; rank_q is the position of the first relevant result for query q (1 ÷ rank_q is taken as 0 if none is retrieved, or if none appears in the top k for MRR@k). Rewards getting one right answer near the top.
used_for: Question answering and passage retrieval (MS MARCO's official metric is MRR@10), conversational search, entity linking, code search. Book: only here.

name: Recall@k, precision@k and hit rate@k
formula: Recall@k = |relevant ∩ top k| ÷ |relevant| ; Precision@k = |relevant ∩ top k| ÷ k ; HitRate@k = (1 ÷ |U|) × sum over users u of 1[at least one relevant item in u's top k]
meaning: relevant is the set of items (or passages) that are actually relevant for a user or query; top k is the system's first k results; ∩ means 'in both sets' and |...| counts elements; U is the set of users or queries; 1[...] is 1 if the condition holds. Recall@k asks how much of what matters was retrieved; precision@k how much of what was shown matters; hit rate asks whether anything relevant was shown (with exactly one held-out item it equals Recall@k).
used_for: Evaluating RAG retrievers (is the needed passage in the top 5 or 20 chunks handed to the LLM?), candidate generation in recommenders, leave-one-out recommendation benchmarks. Book: Chapter 51 (precision at k and recall at k), Chapter 27.

name: Pairwise learning to rank (RankNet and LambdaRank)
formula: P_ij = sigmoid(σ × (s_i − s_j)) ; RankNet loss = −P_bar_ij × ln(P_ij) − (1 − P_bar_ij) × ln(1 − P_ij) ; LambdaRank gradient λ_ij = −σ ÷ (1 + exp(σ × (s_i − s_j))) × |ΔNDCG_ij|
meaning: s_i and s_j are model scores for documents i and j on the same query; σ (sigma) sets the sigmoid's steepness; P_bar_ij is the target (1 if i is more relevant than j, 0 if less, 0.5 if tied); |ΔNDCG_ij| is how much NDCG would change if i and j swapped places, so pairs near the top of the list get larger gradients. LambdaMART trains gradient-boosted trees with these λ gradients.
used_for: Web-search ranking (LambdaMART, from Burges and colleagues at Microsoft Research, won the 2010 Yahoo! Learning to Rank Challenge), e-commerce search, LightGBM objective='lambdarank' and XGBoost rank:ndcg; pairwise ranking losses also train rerankers. Book: only here.

name: Position-based click model and inverse propensity weighting for ranking
formula: P(click on item d shown at position k) = θ_k × γ_d ; unbiased learning-to-rank weight for a click at position k = 1 ÷ θ_k
meaning: θ_k (theta) is the probability that a user examines position k (falls off down the page); γ_d (gamma) is the probability the user clicks item d once examined (its attractiveness or relevance). Clicks on low positions are rarer partly because they are seen less, so weighting each click by 1 ÷ θ_k corrects the logged data before training. θ_k is estimated with randomized swaps or EM. Cascade and dynamic Bayesian network click models are richer variants.
used_for: Training search and feed rankers from click logs without position bias, evaluating ads and recommendations offline. Book: Chapter 51 (position bias), Chapter 31.

name: Multi-objective ranking score
formula: score(u, i) = sum over actions a of w_a × P_hat(a given u, i)
meaning: P_hat(a given u, i) is the ranking model's predicted probability (or expected amount) that user u takes action a on item i, such as click, like, share, reply, long watch, or 'not interested'; w_a are business-chosen weights (negative for negative feedback). The final feed is sorted by this weighted sum, then re-ranked for diversity and policy rules.
used_for: Feed ranking at large platforms: X open-sourced a ranker in 2023 that combines predicted engagement probabilities with fixed weights; YouTube's multi-task ranking (Zhao et al., 2019) combines several predicted objectives the same way. Book: Chapter 51 (stage 2: ranking, a model that predicts many things at once; what feeds optimize).

name: Ad ranking by expected value and generalized second-price pricing
formula: ad rank = bid × pCTR (× quality factors) ; eCPM = 1,000 × bid × pCTR ; GSP price per click for slot 1 = bid_2 × pCTR_2 ÷ pCTR_1 (plus a minimum increment)
meaning: bid is what the advertiser offers per click; pCTR is the predicted click-through probability from the click model; eCPM is expected revenue per thousand impressions; in the generalized second-price auction each winner pays just enough to keep its position, the next advertiser's ad rank divided by its own pCTR. Auction theory itself (Vickrey, incentive compatibility) is covered with game theory.
used_for: Search and display advertising at Google, Meta, Amazon and others; real-time bidding exchanges; why click prediction must be well calibrated. Book: Chapter 51 (the auction, worked by hand; predicting the click), Chapter 48 (second-price auctions).

name: Maximal marginal relevance (diversity re-ranking)
formula: next item = argmax over candidates d not yet selected of [λ × sim(d, q) − (1 − λ) × max over selected d' of sim(d, d')]
meaning: q is the query (or user); sim is a similarity such as cosine of embeddings; the selected set starts empty and grows one item at a time; λ (lambda) between 0 and 1 trades relevance (λ = 1) against novelty relative to what is already chosen. A related diversity metric is intra-list diversity, the average of (1 − sim) over all pairs in a list.
used_for: Diversifying search results and feeds (re-ranking stage), choosing non-redundant chunks for RAG (the MMR retriever option in LangChain and vector databases), extractive summarization. Book: only here (Chapter 51 describes re-ranking for diversity in words).

name: TF-IDF weighting
formula: tfidf(t, d) = tf(t, d) × idf(t), with idf(t) = ln(N ÷ df(t)) ; scikit-learn smoothed idf(t) = ln((1 + N) ÷ (1 + df(t))) + 1
meaning: tf(t, d) is how often term t occurs in document d (sometimes 1 + ln(tf) to damp repeats); N is the number of documents; df(t) is how many documents contain t, so rare terms get high idf. Documents and queries become tf-idf vectors, usually normalized to length 1 and compared by cosine similarity.
used_for: Classic keyword search and text classification features, keyword extraction, a cheap baseline for retrieval and deduplication; the ancestor of BM25. Book: Chapter 11 (TF-IDF), Chapter 27.

name: BM25 ranking function
formula: score(D, Q) = sum over query terms q of IDF(q) × f(q, D) × (k1 + 1) ÷ (f(q, D) + k1 × (1 − b + b × |D| ÷ avgdl)) ; IDF(q) = ln(1 + (N − n(q) + 0.5) ÷ (n(q) + 0.5))
meaning: f(q, D) is how often term q occurs in document D; |D| is the document's length in words and avgdl the average length in the collection; N is the number of documents and n(q) the number containing q; k1 (typically 1.2 to 2.0) controls how fast repeated terms saturate; b (typically 0.75) controls length normalization. The IDF shown is Lucene's non-negative form; Lucene and Elasticsearch also drop the constant (k1 + 1) factor, which does not change rankings. BM25F extends it to weighted fields.
used_for: Default ranking in Lucene, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and Solr; the sparse half of hybrid search in RAG (for example Anthropic's 2024 Contextual Retrieval combined contextual BM25 with embeddings); the standard baseline in the BEIR benchmark. Book: Chapter 27 (BM25, hybrid search), Chapter 51.

name: Cosine similarity (and its link to dot product and Euclidean distance)
formula: cos(a, b) = (a · b) ÷ (length(a) × length(b)) ; for unit-length vectors: length(a − b)^2 = 2 − 2 × cos(a, b)
meaning: a and b are vectors (embeddings, tf-idf vectors); a · b is the dot product; length is the Euclidean norm. Cosine is 1 for the same direction, 0 for unrelated (perpendicular), −1 for opposite; cosine distance = 1 − cos. When embeddings are normalized to length 1, ranking by dot product, cosine or Euclidean distance gives the same order, which is why vector databases offer all three.
used_for: Semantic search and RAG retrieval with embedding models, deduplication by embedding similarity, recommendation similarity, evaluation by embedding similarity. Book: Appendix B (cosine similarity), Chapter 27 (cosine similarity in the RAG loop), Chapter 5.

name: Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF)
formula: RRF(d) = sum over rankers r of 1 ÷ (k + rank_r(d)), with k = 60
meaning: rank_r(d) is document d's position in ranker r's list (1 for the top; documents missing from a list contribute nothing); k is a smoothing constant (60 in the original paper by Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher, 2009) that limits the dominance of top ranks. Results are sorted by the fused score. It needs no score calibration between rankers. Alternative: a convex combination α × normalized dense score + (1 − α) × normalized sparse score.
used_for: Hybrid search that merges keyword (BM25) and vector results in Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Azure AI Search, Weaviate, Qdrant and many RAG pipelines; merging results from several query rewrites. Book: Chapter 27 (reciprocal rank fusion).

name: Approximate nearest neighbor recall@k
formula: recall@k = |ANN top k ∩ exact top k| ÷ k
meaning: ANN top k is the set of k neighbors returned by an approximate index (HNSW, IVF, product quantization); exact top k is the true k nearest neighbors found by brute-force search; |...| counts the overlap. Index settings (efSearch, nprobe) trade this recall against queries per second and memory; results are plotted as recall-versus-throughput curves.
used_for: Tuning and benchmarking vector databases and libraries (FAISS, ScaNN, HNSWlib, ann-benchmarks, big-ann-benchmarks); RAG systems typically target recall around 0.9 to 0.99. Book: Chapter 27 (ANN search; HNSW), Chapter 51.

name: Product quantization and IVF-PQ distance
formula: code size = M × log2(K) bits per vector ; distance(q, x)^2 ≈ sum over m = 1..M of length(q_m − c_m(x))^2 ; IVF search cost ≈ (nprobe ÷ nlist) × N distance computations
meaning: Each vector x is split into M sub-vectors; sub-vector m is replaced by the nearest of K centroids learned by k-means (c_m(x)), so x is stored as M small codes. A query q is compared asymmetrically: its exact sub-vectors q_m against the stored centroids, using M precomputed lookup tables. An inverted-file (IVF) index first clusters the N vectors into nlist lists and scans only the nprobe nearest lists. Variants: optimized PQ (rotation first), ScaNN's anisotropic quantization, scalar and binary quantization (Hamming distance).
used_for: Billion-scale vector search in FAISS (IVF-PQ), Google ScaNN and Vertex AI Vector Search, Milvus and other vector databases; compressing embedding stores for RAG. Book: only here (Chapter 27 covers approximate search in words).

name: HNSW (hierarchical navigable small world) level assignment
formula: level = floor(−ln(u) × m_L), with u uniform between 0 and 1 and m_L = 1 ÷ ln(M)
meaning: Each new vector gets a random top level from this exponentially decaying distribution, so higher layers hold exponentially fewer nodes; M is the number of neighbor links per node; floor rounds down. A search starts at the sparse top layer, walks greedily toward the query, and descends layer by layer, keeping a candidate list of size efSearch at the bottom; search cost grows roughly with the logarithm of the collection size.
used_for: The most widely deployed vector-index algorithm (Malkov and Yashunin, 2016/2018): HNSWlib, FAISS, pgvector, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, Redis. Book: Chapter 27 (HNSW), Chapter 51.

name: Late interaction (ColBERT MaxSim) scoring
formula: score(q, d) = sum over query tokens i of max over document tokens j of (E_q,i · E_d,j)
meaning: E_q,i is the embedding of query token i and E_d,j of document token j (both normalized), produced by a Transformer encoder; each query token finds its best-matching document token, and the matches are summed. Finer-grained than one vector per document, cheaper than a full cross-encoder because document token embeddings are precomputed.
used_for: ColBERT and ColBERTv2/PLAID retrievers (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020), ColPali-style retrieval over page images of PDFs, rerankers in RAG pipelines (RAGatouille, Vespa, Qdrant multivector support). Book: only here.

name: Learned sparse retrieval term weights (SPLADE)
formula: w_j = max over input tokens i of ln(1 + ReLU(w_ij)) ; score(q, d) = sum over vocabulary terms j of w_j(q) × w_j(d)
meaning: w_ij is the masked-language-model logit for vocabulary term j at input position i; ReLU zeros negatives and ln(1 + ...) damps large values; the result is a sparse vector over the vocabulary (including expansion terms not in the text), stored in an ordinary inverted index. The original SPLADE summed over positions, SPLADE v2 and later use the max; training adds a FLOPS regularizer, sum over j of (average over the batch of w_j)^2, to keep vectors sparse.
used_for: Learned sparse retrieval in production search engines (Elastic's ELSER, OpenSearch neural sparse search) and as the sparse leg of hybrid RAG. Book: only here.

name: Simple moving average
formula: SMA_t = (1 ÷ k) × sum over i = 0..k−1 of y_(t−i)
meaning: y_t is the series value at time t; k is the window length; the forecast for the next step is the average of the last k values. Larger k smooths more but reacts more slowly; a centered moving average estimates the trend for seasonal decomposition.
used_for: Smoothing noisy metrics and loss curves, simple demand forecasts, trend extraction in classical decomposition. Book: Chapter 10 (forecasting time series: 7-day moving average worked as 1,070 ÷ 7 ≈ 153).

name: Exponential smoothing (exponential moving average)
formula: s_t = α × y_t + (1 − α) × s_(t−1) ; forecast y_hat_(t+1) = s_t
meaning: y_t is the new observation; s_t the smoothed level; α (alpha) between 0 and 1 is the smoothing weight (higher reacts faster). Unrolled, the weight on an observation i steps back is α × (1 − α)^i, decaying exponentially. When s_0 = 0, dividing by (1 − (1 − α)^t) removes the startup bias. The same update is used as an exponential moving average of training losses and, with other names, of gradients (Adam's moments) and of model weights, which are covered in the deep-learning section.
used_for: Simple exponential smoothing forecasts (statsmodels, R forecast), smoothed loss curves in training dashboards, monitoring baselines. Book: Chapter 10 (exponential smoothing worked: 0.3 × 120 + 0.7 × 100 = 106).

name: Holt-Winters (trend and seasonal exponential smoothing)
formula: level l_t = α × (y_t − s_(t−m)) + (1 − α) × (l_(t−1) + b_(t−1)) ; trend b_t = β × (l_t − l_(t−1)) + (1 − β) × b_(t−1) ; season s_t = γ × (y_t − l_t) + (1 − γ) × s_(t−m) ; forecast y_hat_(t+h) = l_t + h × b_t + s_(t+h−m×(floor((h−1) ÷ m)+1))
meaning: y_t is the observation; l_t the level, b_t the trend (slope per step) and s_t the seasonal effect; m is the season length (7 for daily data with a weekly cycle, 12 for monthly data); α, β and γ between 0 and 1 are smoothing weights; h is the forecast horizon, and the seasonal index uses the last observed season. This is the additive form; the multiplicative form divides by the season instead of subtracting. Holt's linear method drops the seasonal term; damped trend multiplies the trend by φ^h. Some texts (Hyndman's Forecasting: Principles and Practice) write the seasonal update with y_t − l_(t−1) − b_(t−1) in place of y_t − l_t.
used_for: Classic business and operations forecasting (statsmodels ExponentialSmoothing, R's ets), a strong baseline in forecasting competitions and for time-series foundation models. Book: only here (Chapter 10 decomposes series into trend and seasonality).

name: Autoregressive and ARIMA models
formula: y'_t = c + φ_1 × y'_(t−1) + ... + φ_p × y'_(t−p) + ε_t + θ_1 × ε_(t−1) + ... + θ_q × ε_(t−q), with y'_t = y_t − y_(t−1) applied d times
meaning: y'_t is the series after d rounds of differencing (removing trend); φ_1..φ_p (phi) are the autoregressive weights on past values; θ_1..θ_q (theta) are the moving-average weights on past forecast errors ε (white noise); c is a constant. ARIMA(p, d, q) names the three orders; seasonal ARIMA adds the same terms at lag m; ARIMAX adds outside regressors. AR(1) with |φ_1| < 1 is the simplest stationary case.
used_for: Statistical forecasting in economics, energy and operations (statsmodels, R forecast's auto.arima, pmdarima), baselines for time-series foundation models. Book: Chapter 10 (ARIMA definition).

name: Autocorrelation function
formula: ρ_k = sum over t = k+1..T of (y_t − mean y) × (y_(t−k) − mean y) ÷ sum over t = 1..T of (y_t − mean y)^2
meaning: y_t is the series of length T; k is the lag; ρ_k (rho) is the correlation of the series with itself shifted by k steps, from −1 to 1. Peaks at lag m reveal seasonality; a slow decay suggests a trend (difference first). Values outside about ±1.96 ÷ sqrt(T) are significant for white noise. The partial autocorrelation removes the effect of shorter lags and suggests the AR order p; the Ljung-Box test checks residuals.
used_for: Choosing ARIMA orders, detecting seasonality, checking that forecast residuals are random. Book: only here.

name: Prophet additive forecasting model
formula: y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + ε_t ; s(t) = sum over n = 1..N of (a_n × cos(2π × n × t ÷ P) + b_n × sin(2π × n × t ÷ P))
meaning: g(t) is a piecewise-linear (or logistic) trend with automatically placed changepoints; s(t) is seasonality written as a Fourier series with period P (365.25 for yearly, 7 for weekly) and N harmonic pairs with coefficients a_n and b_n; h(t) adds holiday effects; ε_t is noise. Fit as a regularized regression (Bayesian, with Stan).
used_for: Business forecasting with strong calendar effects (Prophet from Meta, 2017; NeuralProphet), dashboards and capacity planning. Book: Chapter 10 (Prophet named in forecasting).

name: A/B test: lift and two-proportion z-test
formula: lift = (p_B − p_A) ÷ p_A ; z = (p_B − p_A) ÷ sqrt(p_pool × (1 − p_pool) × (1 ÷ n_A + 1 ÷ n_B)), with p_pool = (x_A + x_B) ÷ (n_A + n_B)
meaning: p_A and p_B are the conversion rates (successes x ÷ users n) in control A and treatment B; p_pool is the combined rate; |z| > 1.96 means p < 0.05 (two-sided). For continuous metrics (revenue, watch time) Welch's t-test uses (mean_B − mean_A) ÷ sqrt(s_A^2 ÷ n_A + s_B^2 ÷ n_B). Checking results repeatedly before the planned end inflates false positives; sequential tests correct for that.
used_for: Online experiments for ranking models, product features and prompts at every large platform (Microsoft ExP, Netflix, Meta, Booking); shipping decisions for new recommender or LLM versions, with guardrail metrics. Book: Chapter 51 (online experiments; A/B test), Chapter 10 (rolling out a new model safely).

name: Sample size and minimum detectable effect (A/B tests and evals)
formula: n per group = (z_(1−α/2) + z_(1−β))^2 × (σ_A^2 + σ_B^2) ÷ δ^2 ; rule of thumb n ≈ 16 × σ^2 ÷ δ^2 per group (α = 0.05, 80% power) ; paired eval version: n = (z_(α/2) + z_β)^2 × (ω^2 + σ_A^2 ÷ K_A + σ_B^2 ÷ K_B) ÷ δ^2
meaning: δ (delta) is the smallest difference worth detecting (minimum detectable effect); σ^2 is the metric's variance per unit (p × (1 − p) for a conversion rate); α is the false-positive rate and 1 − β the power; z values are standard normal quantiles (1.96 and 0.84). In the eval version from Miller (2024), n is the number of questions, ω^2 = Var(x_A) + Var(x_B) − 2 × Cov(x_A, x_B) is the variance of the paired difference in per-question expected scores, σ_A^2 and σ_B^2 are average within-question sampling variances and K_A, K_B the number of answers sampled per question (more samples per question shrink only that part of the noise); in that paper's notation z_p is the (1 − p) percentile of the standard normal, so z_(α/2) = 1.96 for α = 0.05.
used_for: Planning experiment duration and traffic on A/B platforms; sizing evaluation sets and samples-per-question for model comparisons. Book: only here.

name: CUPED variance reduction
formula: Y_cv = Y − θ × (X − mean X), with θ = Cov(X, Y) ÷ Var(X) ; Var(Y_cv) = Var(Y) × (1 − ρ^2)
meaning: Y is the experiment metric per user; X is a covariate measured before the experiment started (often the same metric in the pre-period), unaffected by treatment; θ (theta) is the regression slope of Y on X; ρ (rho) is the correlation between X and Y. Subtracting the predictable part leaves the treatment effect unbiased but shrinks variance, so experiments need fewer users. It is regression adjustment (ANCOVA) in experiment form.
used_for: Standard in large experimentation platforms (introduced at Microsoft by Deng et al., 2013; used at Netflix, Booking, Meta and in commercial tools such as Statsig and Eppo). Book: only here.

name: Average treatment effect (potential outcomes)
formula: ATE = E[Y(1) − Y(0)] ; under randomization ATE_hat = mean of Y over treated − mean of Y over control
meaning: Y(1) and Y(0) are each unit's potential outcomes with and without the treatment (only one is ever observed); E[...] averages over the population. Randomization makes treated and control groups comparable, so the difference in means is unbiased. Related: the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) and conditional effects CATE(x) = E[Y(1) − Y(0) given x], estimated by uplift models and meta-learners.
used_for: The quantity every A/B test estimates; causal analysis of product changes, marketing uplift modeling, policy evaluation. Book: Chapter 51 and Chapter 54 (randomization as the gold standard for cause and effect).

name: Inverse propensity weighting (causal effects and off-policy evaluation)
formula: ATE_hat = (1 ÷ n) × sum over i of [T_i × Y_i ÷ e(x_i) − (1 − T_i) × Y_i ÷ (1 − e(x_i))], with e(x) = P(T = 1 given x) ; IPS value of a new policy V_hat(π) = (1 ÷ n) × sum over i of r_i × π(a_i given x_i) ÷ μ(a_i given x_i)
meaning: T_i is 1 if unit i was treated and 0 if not; Y_i its outcome; e(x) is the propensity score, the probability of treatment given features x (estimated, for example, by logistic regression). In the logged-bandit version, μ is the old policy that chose action a_i (such as which item to show) in context x_i and earned reward r_i; π is the new policy being evaluated. Weighting by inverse probabilities makes the observed sample look like a randomized one. Doubly robust estimators add an outcome model to reduce variance; clipping large weights trades bias for variance.
used_for: Causal analysis of observational data, offline evaluation of new recommender and ad policies from logged data before an A/B test, unbiased learning to rank. Book: only here (Chapter 57 mentions propensities).

name: Difference-in-differences
formula: DiD = (mean Y_treated,after − mean Y_treated,before) − (mean Y_control,after − mean Y_control,before)
meaning: Y is the outcome; the treated group receives a change (a new model in one market, a policy in one region) and the control group does not; subtracting the control group's change removes trends common to both, under the parallel-trends assumption. Usually estimated as a regression with group, period and interaction terms; synthetic control builds a weighted control group instead.
used_for: Measuring the impact of launches that cannot be randomized per user (market-level rollouts, pricing changes), economics studies of AI adoption effects on employment and productivity. Book: only here.

name: Generalized linear models: Poisson regression and iteratively reweighted least squares
formula: g(E[y given x]) = w · x + b; Poisson: μ = exp(w · x + b), L = sum over i of (μ_i − y_i × ln(μ_i)); IRLS: w_new = (X^T × W × X)^(−1) × X^T × W × z, z = X × w + W^(−1) × (y − μ)
meaning: g is the link function; μ the expected count; W the diagonal IRLS weights (μ_i for Poisson, p_i(1 − p_i) for logistic); z the working response.
used_for: Insurance claim-frequency and severity models, count forecasting, statsmodels/R glm (IRLS), scikit-learn PoissonRegressor/TweedieRegressor, LightGBM/XGBoost Poisson objectives. Book: Chapter 10 (generalized linear models, in words).

name: Successive halving and Hyperband budgets
formula: n_i = floor(n × η^(−i)), r_i = r × η^i; Hyperband s_max = floor(log_η(R ÷ r)), bracket s starts ceil((s_max + 1) × η^s ÷ (s + 1)) settings at budget R × η^(−s)
meaning: n settings, minimum budget r, cut factor η, maximum budget R, bracket s.
used_for: Optuna pruners, Ray Tune ASHA, Keras Tuner Hyperband, scikit-learn HalvingGridSearchCV. Book: Chapter 9 (successive halving worked: 27 settings, 108 versus 729 epochs).

name: LIME local surrogate explanation
formula: explanation(x) = argmin over g of [sum over z of π_x(z) × (f(z) − g(z))^2 + Ω(g)], π_x(z) = exp(−D(x, z)^2 ÷ σ^2)
meaning: f the black-box model, g a simple (sparse linear) surrogate, z perturbed inputs, π_x a closeness kernel, Ω a complexity penalty.
used_for: lime library; per-decision explanations in credit, medical and fraud models. Book: Chapter 10 (LIME, in words).

name: DBSCAN density rule (ε-neighborhoods and core points)
formula: N_ε(x) = {z : d(x, z) ≤ ε}; x is core if |N_ε(x)| ≥ minPts; clusters = core points linked through neighborhoods plus border points; the rest is noise
meaning: ε the radius, minPts the crowding threshold (counting the point itself).
used_for: Spatial and GPS clustering, outlier detection, scikit-learn DBSCAN/HDBSCAN; HDBSCAN on UMAP embeddings in BERTopic. Book: Chapter 10 (DBSCAN, in words).

name: Cost-sensitive decision threshold
formula: predict positive if p ≥ t* = C_FP ÷ (C_FP + C_FN); cost(t) = C_FP × FP(t) + C_FN × FN(t)
meaning: p calibrated probability; C_FP and C_FN the costs of a false alarm and a miss.
used_for: Alert thresholds for fraud, screening and moderation classifiers; scikit-learn TunedThresholdClassifierCV (Elkan 2001). Book: Chapter 9 (which mistake costs more, the threshold game).

name: Group fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds, predictive parity, impact ratio)
formula: SR_g = P(y_hat = 1 given g); DP difference = max SR − min SR; impact ratio = SR_g ÷ max SR; equalized odds TPR_A = TPR_B and FPR_A = FPR_B; predictive parity PPV_A = PPV_B; FPR = (prev ÷ (1 − prev)) × ((1 − PPV) ÷ PPV) × TPR
meaning: Selection rates and per-group confusion-matrix rates; prev the group base rate (Chouldechova 2017 identity).
used_for: Fairlearn, AIF360, the four-fifths rule, NYC Local Law 144 bias audits. Book: Chapter 58 (Why 'fair' has several meanings, worked risk-tool example).

name: PageRank and personalized PageRank
formula: PR(p) = (1 − d) ÷ N + d × sum over q linking to p of PR(q) ÷ L(q); personalized: (1 − d) × v_p in place of (1 − d) ÷ N
meaning: d damping factor (0.85), N pages, L(q) out-links of q, v restart distribution on seed nodes.
used_for: Web ranking signal, random-walk recommenders (Twitter WTF, Pinterest Pixie), TextRank, HippoRAG graph retrieval. Book: Chapter 51 (PageRank: votes from important pages, formula in words and four-page worked example).
